answerKey.primaryProblem: Premature discontinuation of ticagrelor (dual antiplatelet therapy) 12 days ago at 5.5 weeks post-DES to LAD for anterior STEMI, placing patient at high risk for stent thrombosis; compounded by non-adherence to cardiac rehab, LDL above goal, untreated depressive symptoms, continued smoking, and return to high physical/emotional stress without GDMT optimization.
differential: Early DAPT discontinuation with risk of stent thrombosis (most urgent)
Post-MI depression/adjustment disorder vs anxiety-driven exertional avoidance
Suboptimal lipid control (LDL 96 vs goal <55-70) needing statin intensification or add-on therapy
Possible beta-blocker underdosing contributing to residual tachycardia/exertional symptoms
Medication cost/affordability barrier as root cause of nonadherence rather than true intolerance
keyFindings: Pharmacy refill history shows ticagrelor filled only once at discharge, no refill in 6 weeks, despite patient stating he is 'taking everything'
Patient self-reports stopping ticagrelor 12 days ago due to perceived breathlessness side effect and cost
LVEF 40% at discharge with anteroapical/anteroseptal hypokinesis - reduced EF requiring ongoing GDMT and surveillance
PHQ screen positive for moderate depressive symptoms, no active suicidal ideation
Smoking continues at a likely underestimated rate ('a few' vs probable half pack/day)
Returned to 14-hour work days with high stress and avoidance of all exertion due to fear
plan: Urgently address DAPT gap: clarify true discontinuation date, assess chest pain/ischemic symptoms now, and restart dual antiplatelet therapy immediately given high stent thrombosis risk within first weeks-months of DES; if ticagrelor truly intolerable (dyspnea), discuss switching to clopidogrel 75mg (with cardiology-directed loading if indicated) rather than stopping antiplatelet coverage entirely
Investigate and address cost barrier: engage pharmacy/social work for patient assistance program or formulary alternative; explore copay card for ticagrelor or transition plan
Reinforce absolute necessity of DAPT for a minimum of 12 months post-DES (per cath report and current DES guidelines); use teach-back to confirm understanding
Refer/strongly re-engage with cardiac rehabilitation; address access barriers (work schedule, cost, transportation)
Intensify lipid-lowering therapy: continue high-intensity statin, consider adding ezetimibe given LDL 96 above goal; reinforce diet/lifestyle

Screen result positive for depression - refer to behavioral health/primary care for formal evaluation and treatment; this is outside cardiology's prescribing scope for antidepressants but should be flagged and handed off
Counsel on smoking cessation; offer referral to tobacco cessation program/pharmacotherapy per PCP

Address fear of exertion and sexual activity: provide reassurance based on successful revascularization and EF 40%, encourage graded return to activity via cardiac rehab, discuss safety of resuming sexual activity with stable cardiac status
Titrate GDMT as tolerated: assess for uptitration of metoprolol and lisinopril toward target doses at future visits given reduced EF
Schedule close follow-up (1-2 weeks) to confirm DAPT resumption and monitor for ischemic symptoms
redFlags: Stent thrombosis risk: any new chest pain, pressure, or acute dyspnea must prompt immediate emergency evaluation
Suicidal ideation (denied today but must be reassessed given depressive symptoms)
Signs of heart failure decompensation (orthopnea, PND, rapid weight gain) given reduced EF - none currently present but educate patient to report
educationPoints: Dual antiplatelet therapy after drug-eluting stent must continue for a minimum of 12 months per current DES protocol; premature discontinuation substantially raises stent thrombosis risk, which carries high mortality
Medication cost and perceived side effects are common, under-disclosed reasons for nonadherence; proactively asking about affordability and side effects, and offering alternatives, improves adherence
Post-MI depression and anxiety are common and under-recognized; routine screening is part of comprehensive cardiac care
Discrepancy between patient-reported adherence and pharmacy refill data is a teaching moment for using objective adherence data respectfully, without accusation
Reduced EF (40%) after anterior STEMI requires ongoing GDMT titration and surveillance, not just antiplatelet therapy
Cardiac rehabilitation improves outcomes and should be actively encouraged and barriers addressed
Secondary prevention LDL goals after ACS are more aggressive (<55-70 mg/dL) than primary prevention

artifacts.title: Transthoracic Echocardiogram - Discharge
artifacts.author: Echo Lab, Cardiology
artifacts.body: LEFT VENTRICLE: Mildly to moderately reduced systolic function. LVEF estimated 40% by biplane Simpson's method. Regional wall motion abnormality with hypokinesis of the anteroapical and anteroseptal segments, consistent with recent LAD territory infarction. No LV thrombus identified. LV wall thickness normal. VALVES: Trace mitral regurgitation, otherwise structurally normal valves. LEFT ATRIUM: Mildly dilated. RIGHT HEART: Normal size and function, estimated RVSP normal. PERICARDIUM: No effusion. IMPRESSION: Mildly to moderately reduced LVEF (40%) with anteroapical/anteroseptal hypokinesis consistent with recent anterior STEMI. Recommend repeat echo in 3 months to reassess EF and consider ICD evaluation if EF remains ≤35% on GDMT.

artifacts.title: Cardiac Catheterization Report
artifacts.author: Interventional Cardiology
artifacts.body: INDICATION: Anterior STEMI. FINDINGS: Left main - no significant disease. LAD - 100% thrombotic occlusion of the proximal LAD. LCx - mild luminal irregularities, no significant stenosis. RCA - no significant disease. INTERVENTION: Successful primary PCI of the proximal LAD with placement of one drug-eluting stent. Final angiography demonstrated TIMI 3 flow, no residual stenosis, no dissection. Door-to-balloon time 58 minutes. RECOMMENDATION: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + ticagrelor) for minimum 12 months per current DES protocol given proximal LAD location and large territory at risk. High-intensity statin, beta-blocker, and ACE inhibitor per post-MI guideline-directed therapy.

facts.chart: Patient presents for scheduled 6-week follow-up after anterior STEMI and LAD stent placement
facts.says: I'm here for my follow-up after the heart attack thing. I'm doing okay, just checking in like they told me to.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he is taking all his medications, 'every pill, every day'
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history (d2) shows ticagrelor was filled only once at discharge 6 weeks ago with no subsequent refill, while all other medications show regular on-schedule refills
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely believe or present that they are adherent while objective pharmacy data reveals a specific gap; reconciling self-report against refill history without judgment is essential, especially for medications with narrow safety margins like DAPT after DES

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially minimizes smoking as 'a few here and there,' then on further questioning admits to about half a pack per day
mismatches.recordEvidence: No separate smoking-cessation lab exists, but the discrepancy itself (initial minimization vs. reluctant-tier fuller disclosure) demonstrates the pattern of underreporting high-risk behaviors; home HR log (d7) shows intermittent HR spikes to 104-110 bpm on certain days potentially consistent with nicotine/stimulant effect or anxiety, prompting further exploration
mismatches.teachingPoint: Initial self-reports of smoking or substance use are often minimized; direct, non-judgmental follow-up questioning ('how many exactly, counting them up') often reveals a more accurate picture critical for risk stratification

objectives.text: Elicit and reconcile a discrepancy between patient-reported medication adherence and objective pharmacy refill data, specifically identifying premature ticagrelor discontinuation

Recognize the clinical urgency of early DAPT discontinuation after drug-eluting stent placement and formulate an appropriate management plan (resume therapy or substitute agent) within cardiology scope
Screen for and identify post-MI depression and fear-avoidance behavior affecting quality of life, exercise tolerance, and intimacy, while recognizing need for behavioral health referral
Assess modifiable cardiovascular risk factors including lipid control, smoking, and cardiac rehabilitation engagement, and formulate guideline-directed secondary prevention plan
Integrate echocardiographic and catheterization data (reduced EF, anterior wall motion abnormality, stent location) to contextualize ongoing GDMT needs and surveillance plan
Demonstrate respectful, non-judgmental exploration of sensitive topics (cost barriers, sexual activity, mood, smoking) using progressive rapport-building rather than direct confrontation

patient.name: Dennis Papadakis
patient.appearance: Stocky build, salt-and-pepper hair, wearing a plain polo shirt; appears to be seated in a small office at the back of his restaurant with a desk and stacked boxes visible behind him, lighting slightly dim. He smiles frequently and gestures with his hands while talking, but his eyes look tired and his smile sometimes doesn't reach them.

persona.personality: Warm, proud, and used to being the one who takes care of others; deflects vulnerability with humor and bravado
persona.communicationStyle: Talkative and friendly, tends to minimize problems and crack jokes when conversation turns serious; speaks in a direct, informal Midwestern-with-Greek-family-inflection style
persona.emotionalState: Outwardly upbeat and jovial but underlying fatigue, fear, and low mood become apparent with gentle probing
persona.background: Immigrated with his parents as a child; took over the family Greek restaurant from his father 20 years ago; works long hours, proud of providing for his wife and two adult children; the heart attack happened on a busy Saturday night shift
speechExamples: Doc, I'm telling you, I'm tough as an old goat, don't you worry about me.
Everything's good, good, good! Business is picking back up too.
Eh, that pill, it just didn't agree with me, that's all.
My wife keeps telling me to slow down, but you know restaurant people, we don't know how to slow down.
I don't like talking about the sad stuff, doc, let's talk about something else.
concerns: I've been feeling short of breath—could it be from one of the pills?
The medications are really expensive and I'm not sure I can keep paying for all of them.
I'm worried that if I exercise too much or have sex, it might bring on another heart attack.
Am I ever going to feel normal again, or is this just how life is now?

scenario.studentBrief: You are a cardiology fellow conducting a telehealth follow-up visit with Dennis Papadakis, a 55-year-old man who is 6 weeks status post anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI and drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD. He was discharged on aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate, and lisinopril, with an echocardiogram showing LVEF 40%. He is calling from his restaurant. Review his history, assess his recovery, and reconcile the medical record with his self-report.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Six-week follow-up after anterior STEMI and LAD drug-eluting stent placement
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, good to see you! I'm here for my follow-up after the heart attack thing. I'm doing okay, just checking in like they told me to.
tasks: Take a focused interval history including symptoms, functional status, and medication adherence
Review pharmacy records and reconcile the medication list with the patient
Screen for mood symptoms and assess psychosocial adjustment
Review investigation results to guide secondary prevention recommendations
Formulate and communicate a management plan and arrange appropriate follow-up

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at a small office in the back of his restaurant in Chicago, Illinois
profile.summary: A 55-year-old restaurant owner presents for routine 6-week cardiology follow-up after anterior STEMI with drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD, outwardly reporting full recovery and medication adherence. The case teaches fellows to reconcile pharmacy refill data against patient self-report (revealing premature ticagrelor discontinuation with high stent-thrombosis risk) and to screen beneath a jovial exterior for post-MI depression, fear-avoidance, and sexual dysfunction requiring sensitive exploration and appropriate referral.
profile.title: Six-Week Post-STEMI Follow-Up: Hidden DAPT Discontinuation and Post-MI Depression
